opening.headline: Learn how to identify and enumerate all paths where external text enters, and establish justification for prioritizing defenses.
body: Let's consider an agent that searches internal documents, reads the web, summarizes emails, and connects to external MCP servers. The security team has a fixed defense budget for one quarter, yet there appear to be dozens of places that need to be blocked. If there is no list identifying where the entry points are, then it's impossible to determine where to begin defending.

In this class, we first examine the concept of attack surfaces and the analysis procedure described by OWASP. Next, we apply this procedure to LLM systems, distinguishing user inputs, search documents, web pages, tool results, and MCP server outputs as separate entry points. Finally, we trace the entire path from hidden instructions in search documents to tool calls.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can describe the procedures for attack surface analysis and threat modeling.
User input, search documents, web pages, tool results, and MCP server can be distinguished as separate attack surfaces.

screens.title: Where should we start blocking?
screens.lead: First, read the scenario that the security team encountered. The arrows with question marks indicate entrances whose identities are still unknown.

visual.alt: Scene showing six arrows converging around the model box in the agent diagram, with question marks attached.

paragraphs: There is an internal support agent that searches internal documents to generate answers, reads web pages, summarizes received emails, and also uses tools provided by external MCP servers. The security team's request is simple: ensure the system is securely implemented this quarter.

The issue is that there seem to be too many potential entry points. Without a clear list detailing which paths specific inputs take to reach the model, there is no basis for determining where to allocate budget first. Typically, when such situations arise, people begin by inspecting the most prominent user input fields; however, merely monitoring those fields may not be sufficient.
The question this lesson aims to answer is one: how do we locate and count the entrance, and how do we then assign an order based on that result?

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: Without a list of entry points, there can be no justification for allocating defense budgets anywhere. Creating such a list is the first step in defense.

screens.outro: Now let us count the entrances directly while recalling your system.

screens.title: Recall the input pathway of our system
screens.lead: When you select a question, the instructor's thought process is displayed. Please first think through your answer mentally before clicking.

items.prompt: How many pathways are there into our system for external text?
items.answer: At first, you might only think of one user input field. However, documents retrieved through search, web pages browsed, results returned by tools, and tool descriptions sent by external servers—all of these are texts that the model reads. By the end of this class, you'll be able to distinguish and count five or more distinct sources.

items.prompt: Besides the sentences typed into the input field by the user, what else is present in the text that the model reads?
items.answer: The model reads the system prompt, user message, retrieved documents, and tool results as plain text within the same context. The model does not have any indication of who authored each piece of text. Therefore, I must separately track where text I did not write originates.

items.prompt: Who wrote the document retrieved by the tool?
items.answer: Most of the content our team has written is not under our control. External wikis, web pages, customer emails, and third-party API responses are not authored by us and thus are not under our control. If content authored by someone outside our control enters the model's context, that pathway becomes an entry point through which an attacker could exert influence.

screens.outro: It's okay if your mental list is short. Let's examine the predefined procedure for finding the entrance.

screens.title: Attack Surface Analysis Procedure
screens.lead: After clicking the Start button, select the right arrow to advance step by step. Follow along and consider how the table is filled at each step.

steps.title: What is an attack surface?
steps.body: OWASP describes attack surface as all points at which an attacker could gain access to a system and extract data, including every path through which data and commands travel, the code that guards those paths, the valuable data processed by the system, and the code that protects that data. For a web application, entry points include UI forms, HTTP headers and cookies, APIs, files, databases, and messages.

steps.title: Step 1: List the entrances
steps.body: First, we list all points where data and commands flow in and out of the system. It doesn't need to be a perfect list. Missing items can be added later when the configuration changes. Without this list, the subsequent steps cannot begin.

steps.title: Step 2: Group by type
steps.body: The number of entry points can be in the thousands, making it impossible to examine each one individually. OWASP recommends grouping similar items based on whether they are exposed externally or internally, their purpose, implementation, design, and technology. For example, API endpoints are grouped together, while file uploads are grouped separately.

steps.title: Step 3: Count the number for each type
steps.body: It counts how many entrances each group has. The number shows which type is larger and serves as a basis for comparing how much the surface area has increased when new features are added. Creating another page with the same design and technology increases surface area but does not significantly change the nature of risk.

steps.title: Step 4: Select a representative example for focused inspection.
steps.body: We select a few representative cases from each type for in-depth examination. Since instances of the same type often share similar vulnerabilities, we can gain a general understanding of the risks even without knowing all endpoints. When a new type emerges, a more thorough risk assessment becomes necessary.

steps.title: When changes occur, do it again.
steps.body: The source material recommends reviewing what has changed, what has been modified, and what new gaps or vulnerabilities have been introduced. This includes, but is not limited to, authentication and authorization logic, code handling encryption and secret values, and changes to the architecture's trust relationships. Also part of this process is cleaning up unused features and obsolete backups to reduce surface area.

screens.outro: Since we've verified the procedure, let's now examine the architecture to determine where the entrance point of the LLM system is located.

screens.title: LLM System Input Path Inventory
screens.lead: When you select the number marker of the diagram, a window that describes the source and risk of that entrance will open. Please check all five locations.

visual.alt: Agent configuration diagram with five input paths entering the central model box.
labels: Model context (place where the same text is read)

markers.label: user input
markers.title: A prompt written directly by the user
markers.body: This is the most prominent entrance. Since the author is the logged-in user, it's easy to track who made the entry. However, this is only one of the five entrances. As long as the input field is protected, the other four remain open.

markers.label: search document
markers.title: Document retrieved from RAG repository
markers.body: Retrieval attaches similar documents to the context of a query. If the repository contains both internal documents and external wiki or collaboration tool entries, then the person who authored those entries becomes the one whose text the model reads. It is necessary to verify the scope of document authors and individuals who can edit documents.

markers.label: web page
markers.title: Body text read by browsing
markers.body: If the model reads a web page, it will receive the text written by the page's owner exactly as it appears. Hidden text not visible on the screen can also be transmitted to the model as text. If the site is outside our control, we must assume that any content could potentially be present.

markers.label: tool results
markers.title: API response, file content, email body
markers.body: When a tool is invoked, its output is returned into the context. For example, if it's a mail summary tool, the body written by the sender is returned; if it's a file tool, the text written in the file is returned. While the tool itself may be secure, the content it retrieves could be text written by a third party.

markers.label: MCP Server·Extension
markers.title: Tools and explanations provided by external servers
markers.body: The MCP server or extension retrieves the tool's name, description, and execution results from external sources. The description text also serves as an input that the model reads. It is essential to jointly verify whether the provider is trustworthy and whether the server could be altered or tampered with.

screens.outro: All five share the commonality that they are read as text within the same model context.

screens.title: The Four Questions of Threat Modeling and the Supply Chain
screens.lead: Select an item title to expand the content. In sequence, verify what the four key questions of threat modeling mean in an LLM system, and why the supply chain is the entry point.

items.title: Threat modeling is an iterative process.
items.body: OWASP describes threat modeling as a structured, iterative procedure for modeling a system from a security perspective, identifying threats, and defining responses. It is ideal to perform this during the design phase early on, and the documentation should not be done once and then discarded, but rather be maintained and updated alongside the system.

items.title: Question 1 and 2: What is being created, and what could go wrong?
items.body: The first question involves drawing a system diagram showing its architecture and data flow. The entrance inventory we created earlier corresponds to this step. The second question asks what might happen at each entrance of the diagram. In an LLM system, a typical example is when hidden instructions in external text are translated into tool calls.

items.title: Questions 3 and 4: How did you respond, and were you sufficient in your response?
items.body: The third question is determining one of the following actions for each threat: mitigate, eliminate, shift, or accept. The fourth question is reviewing, together with stakeholders, whether the established response is actually sufficient. The response must be testable, and when the system changes, this process returns to these questions.

items.title: The supply chain is also an entrance point (LLM03)
items.body: OWASP LLM03 explains that third-party pre-trained models, datasets, and fine-tuning adapters such as LoRA can be tampered with or corrupted. Since models are binary black boxes, static analysis can only cover a limited scope, and there are currently no strong mechanisms to guarantee the provenance of deployed models. Not only the text input at runtime, but also the components that constitute the system must be included in the inventory.

items.title: Core elements of Google SAIF
items.body: SAIF proposes six core elements as a conceptual framework for making AI systems safe. These include extending security foundations into the AI ecosystem, expanding threat detection and response into AI capabilities, automating defense mechanisms, harmonizing platform-level controls, adjusting controls to enable rapid feedback, and understanding AI risks within business processes.

screens.outro: With both entrance and procedures in place, let's follow one path all the way through.

screens.title: Explanation: The hidden directive in the search document leads to the tool.
screens.lead: The instructor demonstrates solving one attack path. Press the start button and advance step by step using arrows, while simultaneously verifying the controls that can be severed at each point.

visual.alt: Five-step pathway diagram involving search, model, and mail tools from external wiki documents, transmitted externally.
labels: Search adds the document to the context

steps.title: Context: Summary agent has mail tool as well.
steps.body: The internal support agent summarizes search results to provide answers. The same agent can also use a mail transmission tool. While both functions may seem necessary for work, together they can link the functionality of reading documents to sending them externally.

steps.title: Stage 1: The attacker implants instructions into the document.
steps.body: The attacker hides a sentence targeting the model in one external wiki document. For example, they insert a sentence that appears ordinary to a person—such as a document summary followed by a directive to send the result to a specific address—at the end of the document. At this stage, the attacker does not connect to our system; they only modified the text we read.

steps.title: Step 2: Search inserts the document into the context.
steps.body: When a user poses a relevant question, the search selects that document to be attached to the context. At this point, the only feasible control is attribution. By adding attribution to content originating from external sources and by limiting the scope of individuals who can access and store the repository, the risks associated with this entry point are reduced.

steps.title: Step 3: The model reads sentences within the document as instructions.
steps.body: The model reads the sentences written in the document and the actions requested by the user using the same characters. Therefore, it is possible to plan mail tool calls by following hidden sentences. One should not expect the model to perfectly distinguish between instructions and data. Relying on this step alone is insufficient.

steps.title: Step 4: If the tool has broad permissions, it is actually transmitted.
steps.body: OWASP LLM06 Excessive Agency explains that when excessive functionality, excessive permissions, and excessive autonomy overlap, manipulated outputs can result in actual harm. The ability to send a read-only agent functionality constitutes excessive functionality, and transmitting without user confirmation constitutes excessive autonomy.

steps.title: Explanation conclusion: Three entrances were connected in a single line.
steps.body: This path consists of three entry points—search documents, models, and tools—arranged in a single line. Breakpoints exist at multiple locations. External source citations are displayed, read-only tools are provided to agents, and high-impact actions such as sending require user approval. Such controls enable inventory management to determine where components should be placed.

screens.outro: I have followed one path to the end, so I will now summarize the key points.

screens.title: Key takeaways
screens.lead: Review once again the core of the lesson, and consider your first step toward applying it to your system.

paragraphs: The attack surface consists of every point where the model reads text. This includes not only user input but also search documents, web pages, tool results, and MCP server outputs. It is this common contextual reading of all these elements as text that differentiates LLM systems.

By grouping entry points by type, a basis for priority is established. Threat modeling is a process of repeatedly asking, together with the system, what is being built, what could go wrong, how to respond, and whether the safeguards are sufficient. Supply chain components such as models and data are also included within entry points.

Going back to the security team at the start of class, a new question now arises. By listing the five entry points and tracing which tools are connected to each, we can see that the path from search documents to email transmission is the one that should be severed first.

callout.label: Points to remember
callout.text: The entrance list is not a one-time document to be created and then finished. It must be updated each time a tool is added or a data source is connected.

glossary.def: It is the set of all entry points through which an attacker could access the system or insert or extract data. In LLM systems, the ingress pathway of external text that the model reads is critical.

It is an iterative procedure of modeling the system from an attacker's perspective to identify threats and define responses, starting during the design phase and continuously updated alongside the system.
A list categorizing and counting the paths through which external text and data enter the system.
Third-party models, datasets, fine-tuning adapters, and packages—collectively refers to all components coming from external sources.
This is a vulnerability where overextended functionalities, permissions, or autonomy in LLMs can be manipulated, leading to harmful behaviors through incorrect outputs.

misconceptions.myth: As long as the user input field is protected, all external inputs are blocked.
misconceptions.fact: The model reads search documents, web pages, tool results, and text provided by the MCP server within the same context. User input is merely one of several entry points.

misconceptions.myth: Threat modeling is something you do once during the design phase.
misconceptions.fact: A threat model is a document maintained and updated alongside a system. When tools or data sources change, return to the questions and review again.

misconceptions.myth: All entrances must be thoroughly understood without exception before analysis can begin.
misconceptions.fact: By grouping entrances by type, counting them, and verifying representative examples, you can identify the broad outline of risks even without knowing all endpoints.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: Any location where external text enters is a potential attack surface.
By grouping entrances by type, a basis for defense priority is established.
Threat modeling is a procedure of iteratively asking the system four questions.
Models and data are also supply chain components, and larger tool privileges can result in greater damage.
closing.reflectionLead: The following questions are for self-thinking purposes only and will not be submitted or graded.
closing.reflection: In our system, how many input paths are there for the model to read text, and where does the text I did not write originate from?

checks.q: The internal support agent uses document summarization, web browsing, and integration with external MCP servers. Which explanation best captures the attack surface?
options: Checking only the prompts entered by the user in the input field covers all external inputs.
All ingress points for external text that the model reads from context (search documents, web pages, tool results, MCP responses, etc.) are entrances.
If rules are written into the system prompt, the entrance may become blocked; therefore, an entrance list is unnecessary.
The only attack surface is points that directly access the model weight files.
checks.explain: The model reads not only user inputs but also search documents, web pages, tool results, and text provided by the MCP server within the same context. Therefore, every place where external text enters serves as an entrance.

wrong.0: User input is merely one of several entry points.
wrong.2: The rules must at least remain in place, and entrance points must be defined in order to establish priorities.
wrong.3: Besides weights, every point where data can be inserted or removed is a surface.

checks.intro: This question examines the functions used by agents to review the entrance point. Results are not recorded.
checks.correctFeedback: Yes. This is the assessment that all external text ingress paths should be considered entry points.
checks.incorrectFeedback: Sorry, the options are mixed up, as if viewed through a narrow lens of user input or weight file.

checks.q: Review the attack surface analysis procedure in the correct order.
items: Grouped by function, design, and technology type
Count the number for each type
Select representative examples by type for focused inspection.
checks.explain: Since there may be thousands of entry points, grouping them by type, counting the occurrences, and selecting representative examples for inspection allows you to identify the risk profile without needing to know all endpoints.
checks.intro: Try setting out the sequence of the analysis procedure. The results are not recorded.
checks.correctFeedback: The order is correct. It proceeds with listing, grouping, counting, and example verification.
checks.incorrectFeedback: The order is incorrect. Remember that you must first group by type before counting the number of items.
